The Spotted dove (Spilopelia chinensis) is a common resident across South and Southeast Asia, yet its developmental physiology under controlled thermal conditions has received limited quantitative attention. Field records indicate that newly laid eggs, incubated at 39 °C [T = 39 °C], produce hatchlings after an incubation period of approximately 14.5 days [ab = approximately 14.5 days], a duration broadly consistent with other tropical columbids of comparable egg size. Upon emergence, the altricial hatchling weighs a mere 7.3 grams [Ww0 = 7.3 grams], a value that reflects the relatively low energetic investment per offspring typical of many dove species. This initial wet weight is notably lower than the mass recorded soon after the first exogenous feeding, when the neonate's body mass rises to an average of 6.4 grams [Wwb = 6.4 grams] — a modest increase driven primarily by the absorption of residual yolk reserves in the first 24 to 36 hours post-hatch. Such a trajectory suggests that the initial days of brooding are critical for the nestling's transition to sustained growth under parental care.

Under the thermal conditions of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], which approximate the internal nest microclimate during active brooding, a predictable sequence of developmental milestones occurs during the nestling period. The chick achieves sustained flight and fledges from the nest at 15 days after hatching [tx = 15 days after hatching], a relatively rapid developmental pace that aligns with the open-cup nesting strategy and associated predation risks faced by this species at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. Following nest departure, the fledgling continues to be provisioned by both parents for an additional period. However, the onset of full reproductive capability occurs considerably later. Puberty, defined as the age at which the gonads become capable of gamete production, is attained at 63 days after hatching [tp = 63 days after hatching] when measured at a stable ambient temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This delay between fledging and sexual maturity allows the juvenile to complete its somatic development, a critical phase during which the bird accumulates the body condition necessary to support future reproductive effort.

First successful breeding in the Spotted dove typically occurs at one year after hatching (365 days after hatching) [tR = 365 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], a timing that aligns with the seasonal onset of suitable nesting conditions in much of its range. The interval between achieving puberty and initiating a first clutch is thus several months, a gap that likely reflects the time required for territory establishment and pair bond formation. In terms of annual reproductive output, available field data indicate that females lay a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], with only one clutch produced each year [F_R_i = one clutch produced each year]. This low fecundity is partly offset by the pair's investment in prolonged biparental care, which improves the survival prospects of each nestling. The reproductive strategy is one of high per-offspring investment and low annual productivity, consistent with the life-history pattern observed in many small- to medium-sized tropical columbids.

In terms of physiological energetics, respirometry trials conducted under normoxic conditions and a controlled ambient temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C] have quantified the basal oxygen consumption of adult Spotted doves at 166.63 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 166.63 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value, which represents the maximum resting metabolic rate measured in post-absorptive adults during their active phase, situates the species within the expected range for a columbid of its body size. There is a notable sexual dimorphism in final adult body mass: females attain an ultimate wet weight of 157.2 grams [Wwi = 157.2 grams], while males grow slightly larger, reaching 163.6 grams [Wwi = 163.6 grams]. This approximately 4 percent difference in mass between the sexes is not extreme by columbid standards, though it may confer advantages in male-male competition for nesting sites. The energetic demands of maintaining this body mass at the elevated temperatures typical of tropical lowlands are considerable, yet the species appears well-adapted to its thermal environment.

Longevity records from wild populations indicate that the maximum lifespan in the Spotted dove is approximately 3577 days [am = approximately 3577 days] when measured under the warm, stable thermal conditions of its native range, a figure derived from banding studies conducted at an average ambient temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This corresponds to nearly ten years, a respectable duration for a bird of this mass and reproductive output, and it suggests that adult mortality rates are relatively low once the vulnerable juvenile stage has been survived. The species' demographic strategy appears to rely on high adult survival and a low, consistent reproductive rate rather than on high fecundity or rapid generational turnover. Comparative analyses with other tropical doves show that this combination of extended lifespan, modest clutch size, and delayed maturation is characteristic of species inhabiting relatively stable, resource-predictable environments. Such life-history traits position the Spotted dove as a classic equilibrium species within its community, well-suited to the competitive, predator-rich ecosystems of the Asian tropics.
